title: Opinion: Consent — and the Courage to Speak Up — Must Be Taught Long Before College
summary: When my 9-year-old son was little, I used to put him in a shirt that said, “Boys will be boys,” but the words were crossed out and underneath it read: “Boys will be good human beings.” That should be the standard — not just for boys, but for all children. And it starts with parents, […]
content: When my 9-year-old son was little, I used to put him in a shirt that said, “Boys will be boys,” but the words were crossed out and underneath it read: “Boys will be good human beings.” That should be the standard — not just for boys, but for all children. And it starts with parents, caregivers, coaches, teachers and every adult who helps shape and raise a child. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Rape whistles, pepper spray and martial arts can be last-minute defenses against sexual assault. But truly preventing sexual violence means starting early and educating children about body safety, boundaries, consent and what to do when they see or know someone else being harmed. The emerging story of gang rape allegations at Cornell University shows why those lessons are vital. In a lawsuit, a now-former student says Chi Phi fraternity members pressured her to consume drugs and alcohol until she was incapable of consent, and that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted her while others discussed what was happening live in a group chat. The criminal investigation has since been taken over by the New York state attorney general’s office after local prosecutors did not charge anyone. Related How The 74 Revealed Decades of Alleged Sexual Abuse in New York Schools This case is yet another call to action: Children must be taught both about consent and to speak up when someone is being harmed, years before they set foot on a college campus. As a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, the founder of a nonprofit that works with families and schools to prevent it, and a mom of 9-year-old twins, this is deeply personal to me. There were 57 boys in that fraternity group chat. Fifty-seven chances for the situation to change. Not one spoke up. That is a failure that starts long before college. Children must be taught that doing the right thing isn’t only about their own behavior. It’s also about what they do when someone else is being harmed — especially when speaking up means going against the group. That starts with giving children clear, practical lessons they can carry with them as they grow. My organization helps educators teach children from an early age that they have the right to say no to an unwanted touch. Just as importantly, we teach children to listen when someone says no to them and to respect that refusal. As they get older, that lesson grows with them: A friend, a date, a teammate or someone they’ve been intimate with before does not owe them access to their body. Consent has meaning only when it’s given freely and affirmatively. It can be withdrawn at any time. And someone who is intoxicated, incapacitated or otherwise unable to make that choice cannot give it. Raising good human beings involves more than teaching children not to hurt someone. They must also be prepared for times when it isn’t their own behavior that is the issue — it’s someone else’s. Related New Research Looks for Ways to Reduce Sexual Harassment and Assault in Schools Doing the right thing gets harder when the person causing harm is a friend, teammate or someone whose acceptance matters. Kids need to know that loyalty does not mean looking the other way. Being part of a team, fraternity or sorority, friend group or group chat does not mean going along with something you know is wrong. Sometimes doing the right thing means being uncomfortable, unpopular or the odd person out — and doing it anyway. Speaking up does not always mean confronting someone directly or putting yourself in danger. It can mean creating a distraction, checking in with the person who may be at risk or getting help from a parent, teacher, counselor, coach or another trusted adult. What matters is that friends or witnesses do something, and that they keep telling until they get the two H’s: Heard and Helped. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. Imagine if just one of 57 frat members at Cornell had decided that protecting another person mattered more than going along with the group. That is the kind of child we should all be trying to raise — boys and girls who know what is right and have the courage to act on it. That’s what it means to be good human beings.

title: Indianapolis Public Schools Proposes Closing 6 Schools Amid Declining Enrollment and Budget Shortfall
summary: Indianapolis Public Schools is proposing to close six schools after this school year as student enrollment plunges and budget problems plague the district. The following schools would be affected, according to information shared at a Tuesday agenda review session of the IPS school board, which is expected to take action on the plan Dec. 8. […]
content: This article was originally published in Chalkbeat Indiana. Indianapolis Public Schools is proposing to close six schools after this school year as student enrollment plunges and budget problems plague the district. The following schools would be affected, according to information shared at a Tuesday agenda review session of the IPS school board, which is expected to take action on the plan Dec. 8. Ralph Waldo Emerson School 58. The school will merge with Christian Park School 82 at Christian Park. Christian Park will continue to offer the Exploratory instructional model. Robert Lee Frost School 106. The school will merge with Eliza Blaker School 55 at Eliza Blaker, which will continue to offer the Reggio-inspired instructional model. Benjamin Harrison School 2. The school will merge with Charity Dye School 27, which will continue to offer the International Baccalaureate (IB) instructional model. Longfellow Middle School. The school will merge with Howe Middle School, which will continue to offer the IB model. Frederick Douglass School 19 and James A. Garfield School 31 will both merge with Eleanor Skillen School 34. Eleanor Skillen will offer the STEM instructional model that James A. Garfield currently offers. Margaret McFarland Learning Academy (MMLA) and Positive Supports Academy will move to James A. Garfield School 31. MMLA will continue to support students with disabilities, while Positive Supports Academy will continue to offer alternative education services. The elementary high-ability program will move from Merle Sidener Academy 59 to the Benjamin Harrison School 2 building, which Johnson described as more central in the district. The new Joyce Kilmer 69 building currently under construction will become the CITY (Central Indiana Training for Youth) Career Center. School closures would take place next summer, and could force families to adjust their plans for the 2027-28 school year — the first round of enrollment for that year closes Dec. 18. Closures would disrupt students’ plans and educational trajectories, and some might choose to leave the district altogether rather than move to another IPS school. If the schools close, families who’ve chosen them during the enrollment window school will be contacted, IPS Superintendent Aleesia Johnson said. Johnson said the district sought to ensure that schools absorbing affected students would be able to accommodate them. “Change of this magnitude is never easy,” Johnson said at the Tuesday agenda review session. The proposed closures would be the most significant in the district since 2023, when IPS closed six schools in a bid to make the district more attractive to families while consolidating its operations. Other closures and consolidations happened in 2008 and 2017. The timing is also significant: The district is set to cede some control over its buildings in 2028 when the Indianapolis Public Education Corporation assumes responsibility for buildings and transportation in IPS and charter schools within its boundaries. Under the proposal up for a board vote, the district would keep its enrollment zones and grade configurations intact, Johnson said. IPS families could choose a different school than the default options within their zone and still receive transportation. A huge factor in the looming school closures is the steep slide in enrollment in IPS in the last several years, a trend occurring in districts across the country. The district has lost roughly a third of its enrollment over the past decade, and the number of students in IPS is now below 20,000. Over the same period, charters have expanded, and combined enrollment in independent charters and those in the district’s Innovation Network now exceeds enrollment in IPS-run schools. Earlier this month, the school board gave the district the go-ahead to start planning school closures following this school year. Shortly after Election Day, IPS Superintendent Aleesia Johnson also said the district had to plan for closures , despite the success of a $95 million tax measure at the polls on Nov. 3 that would provide money for both district-run and charter schools. Even with the success of that ballot measure, the district said it had to close a budget gap with $20 million in cuts. The process differs significantly from what occurred four years ago, when the district spent months gathering and considering public input from the public before the board in 2023 passed what IPS called the Rebuilding Stronger plan , which included the school closures. Notably, two schools slated for closure this year — Frederick Douglass School 19 and Robert Lee Frost 106 — absorbed students from closed schools in 2023 . Johnson noted one factor in the closure timeline is that IPS has a brief window to sell the buildings while the district still controls its buildings and while the state’s $1 building law, which requires districts to offer unused school buildings to charter schools for $1, does not apply to IPS. The sale of these buildings will allow the district to generate needed revenue, she said. The district has recently tried to reassert its authority in a couple of areas. It withdrew from the universal Enroll Indy system for local schools and now uses an enrollment platform run by PowerSchool, a move that angered charters that have also used Enroll Indy. And it is pushing to renegotiate its contracts with Innovation Network schools in order to reflect the true cost to the district of providing them with certain services, IPS leaders said. But neither of those moves solve the broader challenges that are pushing the district towards closures. This story was originally published by Chalkbeat, a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters .

title: Nevada Parents Push Lawmakers for 45-Minute Daily Recess in Elementary Schools
summary: The first time her daughter came home saying she’d missed recess for “study hall,” Brandi Vesco thought nothing of it. But as it continued to happen, she began to see skipped recess as a bigger problem. Vesco found out the school was keeping kids from recess if they hadn’t finished their in-class work. On Wednesdays, […]
content: This article was originally published in Nevada Current. The first time her daughter came home saying she’d missed recess for “study hall,” Brandi Vesco thought nothing of it. But as it continued to happen, she began to see skipped recess as a bigger problem. Vesco found out the school was keeping kids from recess if they hadn’t finished their in-class work. On Wednesdays, the entire school skipped recess for additional instructional time. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter When Vesco complained to the teacher and principal, they began allowing her daughter to go to recess and sending unfinished classwork home. Vesco eventually decided to enroll her daughter at a different public school, 5 minutes away, that gives students 45 minutes of recess each day. She’d found a solution for her daughter, but one thought lingered: What about all the other kids? “Children don’t thrive sitting and trying to learn for long periods of time,” said Vesco, a former ed-tech reporter and the founder of Washoe Parents Coalition. “It’s common sense to me. We all do better with some exercise and movement in our day.” Vesco and the coalition are now advocating that all elementary students receive at least 45 minutes of recess during the school day. They also want to prohibit the withholding of recess for academic or minor disciplinary reasons. An example of a Nevada public school with a policy of withholding recess. (Photo courtesy of Washoe Parents Coalition) They have secured a bipartisan duo of lawmakers — Assemblymembers Alexis Hansen (R-Sparks) and Selena La Rue Hatch (D-Reno) — to sponsor a bill on the issue when the Nevada State Legislature meets next year. Hansen, in a statement to the Nevada Current , said the legislation is a “commonsense, bipartisan effort” that will promote “healthier, happier students who are better prepared to learn.” “Recess isn’t a luxury for children,” she continued. “It’s essential to their physical, emotional, and academic development. Every Nevada elementary school student deserves time during the school day to get outside, move, play, and recharge.” Currently, Nevada law does not require elementary schools to provide any recess time. The Nevada Department of Agriculture’s Nevada School Wellness Policy, which schools that participate in the National School Lunch Program are supposed to adopt, states schools “must provide the opportunity for moderate to vigorous physical activity” for at least 30 minutes during each regular school day. That same policy states that schools shall not withhold opportunities for physical activity as punishment. Related I Research Play – and Here’s Why Recess is Much More Important Than Just a Fun Break Vesco suspects the policy has little teeth, big loopholes, or both. The coalition has been calling on parents to report existing violations of that policy to the state Department of Agriculture or Washoe County School District, which formally adopted the wellness policy. WCSD did not respond to the Current ’s request for comment. The coalition assembled a group of volunteers to call every WCSD elementary school to determine how much recess kids were receiving. They gathered information from 58 of the district’s 66 elementary schools and found that 14 give students 45 minutes or more of recess. They also found that schools in low-income neighborhoods have fewer minutes of recess than schools in higher-income neighborhoods. Low-income schools are also far more likely to not have a physical education teacher. The opportunity to play, to move and to be outside should not be limited to only certain neighborhoods, argues Vesco and other supporters of the national “Say Yes to Recess” movement. Recess is a valuable part of the educational environment, offering space for friendship and connection, problem solving and resilience. “I think our school districts get so caught up on catching kids up on their proficiencies, which we should be doing, that we end up cutting things like recess,” said La Rue Hatch, a public school teacher and mother to an elementary schooler. “But every study actually shows us that if we are taking away their recess time, we’re actually taking away their ability to focus and their ability to learn, and we’re actually going to have significantly more harmful consequences as a result.” While the coalition is based on Washoe, they believe limiting recess is a broader problem for the state. According to Vesco, initial calls to elementary schools within Clark County School District have revealed many offer 20 minutes or less each day. In Douglas County School District, recess time varies from 30 to 55 minutes. Related School Is Back in Session, and Recess Is Having a Moment But it’s not all school districts. In Carson City School District, every elementary school offers 45 minutes. The coalition believes every school can incorporate 45 minutes of recess without making their school day longer or needing additional funding. “It’s about scheduling,” said Vesco. The language of the “Say Yes To Recess” bill has not yet been drafted. But the Nevada Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Children’s Advocacy Alliance, and Nevada Cancer Coalition have already signed onto the cause. Vesco says other groups, including the Nevada State Education Association, which represents teachers and staff across the state, have also signaled support. Advocates point to research showing that early elementary students who got 45 minutes of recess were “less off task and more focused in class” than students who got 30 minutes. While the effort is still in its infancy, Vesco says initial response from parents and the public has been wildly positive: “Most people are like ‘Duh.’ Of course elementary school students can’t be sitting still without movement’” for long stretches. Reporter Jeniffer Solis contributed to this article. Nevada Current is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. Nevada Current maintains editorial independence. Contact Editor Hugh Jackson for questions: info@nevadacurrent.com .

title: ‘Now We Have to Deliver:’ New Texas House Member on Her Education Goals
summary: Democrat Montserrat Garibay, who won Texas House District 49 in this month’s history-making election, told The 74 she has big plans for education when she assumes her new role in January. Garibay will take the seat vacated by Gina Hinojosa, who successfully challenged Republican Greg Abbott for governor, denying the conservative Trump ally a fourth […]
content: Democrat Montserrat Garibay, who won Texas House District 49 in this month’s history-making election, told The 74 she has big plans for education when she assumes her new role in January. Garibay will take the seat vacated by Gina Hinojosa, who successfully challenged Republican Greg Abbott for governor, denying the conservative Trump ally a fourth term and becoming the first Latina to lead the state. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter “I’m really proud and grateful,” Garibay said of her own Nov. 3 victory. “I spent the past year listening to people at their doors, and I am ready to take their stories, their needs and what they’re asking us to change to the Capitol.” And she’s not just celebrating her own success, but that of her party: Democrats took control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. “Seeing Democrats do so well in a state as red as Texas gives me hope and reiterates the power of grassroots organizing,” Garibay said. “I think about the young people we registered who were voting for the first time, the union members who showed up for us, and the volunteers who kept knocking on doors. That’s what democracy looks like to me.” The 47-year-old is walking into this radically changed landscape as a newcomer, having never run for political office before. Garibay was born in Mexico City and came to the United States at age 12, unable to speak English — and without citizenship. She started her post-secondary education at community college before earning her bachelor’s and master’s degrees from the University of Texas at Austin. She later became the vice president for certified employees with Education Austin, a merged local union affiliated with the American Federation of Teachers, the National Education Association and the AFL-CIO . She also served as secretary-treasurer of the Texas AFL-CIO. Incoming House member Montserrat Garibay (left) and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (right) on March 3, 2026, primary day for District 49. Garibay spent eight years as a bilingual pre-K teacher at the Austin Independent School District before serving in the U.S. Department of Education during the Biden-Harris administration, starting in 2022. She was first a senior labor relations advisor before taking over as director of the Office for English Language Acquisition. While there, she led the effort to return the Title III program, which funds and supports English learners, to her office from the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, where it had been for 15 years. “Bringing it back gave the state and local education leaders a team of 16 career staff with expertise in educating English learners,” Garibay said. “We could answer districts’ and states’ questions, share current research and connect educators with professional development they could use in their classrooms.” As for her history with the governor-elect, their shared office is not the first time the two have crossed paths: Hinojosa was the first person Garibay voted for — as an Austin school board candidate in 2012 — after she became a U.S. citizen. She spoke to The 74 a week after the election about the education issues she deems most important. The conversation has been edited for clarity and length. You came to this country unable to speak English. What was that like for you as a student? I remember sitting in class and knowing some of the concepts in Spanish but being unable to explain what I knew in English. I was placed in remedial classes. The language I spoke at home — and all the knowledge I carried in that language — was too often treated as a problem. My ESL teacher, Mrs. Hernandez, changed my experience with school. She gave me challenging work and expected me to do it. She built a relationship with my mother and made school a place where my sister and I felt safe. That combination mattered. I knew I could make mistakes as I learned English, and I knew she expected me to keep learning. I carried that with me when I became a bilingual pre-K teacher in Austin ISD. Related English Learner Programs: Too Easy to Enter, Too Hard to Exit, Educators Say What will be your biggest priorities in education when you assume office in January? Right now, the way our schools get funded is by daily attendance. We want to make sure that we change that to enrollment. (Chronic absenteeism remains a major challenge for schools across the country. It’s also impacts their funding when allocations are based on daily attendance.) Why do you want to rein in vouchers? The 89 th Texas legislature under Gov. Greg Abbott approved $1 billion for the launch of the voucher program for school year 2026-27. The comptroller has already asked lawmakers to double its funding. First-year records showed that at least 70% of students awarded vouchers had previously attended private school or been homeschooled. I oppose expanding the program. I want public reporting of who received vouchers, how providers spend the money and what services participating schools provide to students with disabilities and English learners. My budget priority is to raise the basic allotment and better fund special education and bilingual education in the public schools that serve our communities. Related After Midterm Wave, Democrats Inherit a School Choice Dilemma Tell me more about how you might amplify bilingualism. Being bilingual is a superpower, and in Texas it’s a skill we need every day. Think about a nurse explaining a diagnosis to a parent or a small business owner serving customers in their own language. I want more Texas students to graduate able to do that kind of work in two or more languages. In the legislature, I want to expand access to high-quality dual language programs, invest in recruiting and preparing bilingual teachers and strengthen Texas’s recognition of biliteracy through the Seal of Biliteracy (which honors a high school graduate’s proficiency in two or more languages). I also want school districts, community colleges and employers to work together so students can use their language skills in career and technical education, internships and apprenticeships. Bilingual students can be the next entrepreneurs in our communities, investing and providing services in multiple languages. And what will you do to protect Plyler v. Doe, the landmark 1981 Supreme Court decision that guarantees a student’s right to a public school education regardless of their immigration status? We’re working on a bill right now to make sure we support and protect the access of our students to public education. We’re taking a look at different bills that have happened in New York and different areas. New York passed a bill that really protected Plyer v. Doe . Plyler is the law, but we have seen the attacks on it. Now, with a new governor here in Texas, I think things are going to be different, but I want to make sure that we have those protections no matter what governor we have. That is something that is very dear to me. Related Post-Election Hope for Immigrant Students Dimmed But Not Dead After Miller Named Many young immigrants have seen their hopes for college dashed because the government has taken direct aim at the funding that allows them to attend. What might you do about that? Texas was the first state in our country to offer in-state tuition to qualifying undocumented students. It passed with bipartisan support in 2001, and Gov. (Rick) Perry signed it. It gave students who grew up here and graduated from Texas high schools a chance to pay a rate that made college possible. A federal court order ended that access in 2025. (The Department of Justice sued 27 states and other entities for offering in-state-tuition. Texas did not fight the administration’s edict.) I came to Texas undocumented and was the first in my family to go to college. My sister was in the first class of undocumented students receiving in-state tuition. Education transformed my life. I think about the high school seniors in our district who are now devastated and are trying to figure out how to attend college. I want to help restore an affordable path to those students. They’ve done the work to graduate, and I want them to be able to keep learning, build a career and give back to the communities that raised them. And what about younger kids? I taught bilingual pre-K in Austin ISD for eight years. I saw how much children grow when they have a consistent place to learn, play and build relationships. I also know that a pre-K seat only gets a family so far if the school day ends before a parent’s shift does. I want Texas to expand access to full-day pre-K for 3- and 4-year-olds and increase access to childcare scholarships for working families. Public schools and community childcare providers can partner to offer care before and after the school day. We also need to make sure providers have the resources to pay early educators fairly and keep classrooms open. Families need care they can afford, trust and count on throughout their workday.
